oneLiner: Regulated cell death comes in distinct forms — apoptosis (intrinsic/extrinsic, caspase-driven, non-inflammatory), necroptosis (caspase-independent, lytic, inflammatory), lysosomal/autophagic degradation, and ferroptosis (iron-dependent lipid peroxidation) — distinguished by morphology, machinery and inflammatory outcome.

sections.heading: Why programmed cell death & hallmarks of apoptosis
points: Needed for development/morphogenesis, tissue and immune homeostasis, removal of infected/damaged cells, and response to cellular stress.
Apoptotic morphology: cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, nuclear fragmentation, membrane blebbing (membrane stays intact), apoptotic bodies → phagocytosis.
Biochemical hallmarks: caspase activation, DNA fragmentation, phosphatidylserine (PS) exposure on the outer leaflet.
Caspases cleave cytoskeletal regulators → cortical actin changes → blebbing.
Caspases cleave plasma-membrane phospholipid-transfer proteins → PS flipped to cell surface (eat-me signal for phagocytes).

sections.heading: Caspase cascade
points: Caspases = proteases cleaving selected proteins in regulated death.
Initiator caspases: caspase-8 (extrinsic) and caspase-9 (intrinsic) start the cascade.
Executioner caspases: caspase-3, -6, -7 cleave cellular targets and dismantle the cell.

sections.heading: Intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis & BCL-2 family
points: Internal stimulus induces pro-apoptotic proteins → BAX/BAK activate and oligomerize in mitochondrial outer membrane → MOMP.
Cytochrome c released to cytosol → apoptosome forms → activates initiator caspase-9 → executioners → apoptosis.
Anti-apoptotic BCL-2 (in excess) sequesters pro-apoptotic proteins, blocks BAX/BAK, preserves survival.
BCL-2 family: 3 pro-apoptotic classes (activators, effectors, derepressors/sensitizers) + 1 anti-apoptotic class.
Effectors (BAX/BAK) and anti-apoptotic members have BH1–BH4 domains; activators and sensitizers are BH3-only.

sections.heading: Extrinsic (Fas-mediated) apoptosis
points: Fas ligand binds and clusters Fas death receptor on cell surface.
Adaptor FADD links activated Fas to caspase-8 → DISC (death-inducing signaling complex).
Caspase-8 dimerizes/activates at DISC → cleaves executioner caspases 3 and 7 → apoptosis.

sections.heading: Necroptosis
points: Regulated but caspase-independent, lytic and inflammatory; favored when caspase-8/apoptosis is absent or inhibited.
Morphology: plasma-membrane rupture, cytoplasmic swelling and vacuolization, swollen mitochondria; no condensed, fragmented apoptotic nucleus.
Extrinsic triggers: TNFR1, pattern-recognition receptors TLR3 and TLR4.
Intrinsic trigger: ZBP1 sensing Z-form nucleic acids.
Rupture releases DAMPs → detected by T cells, dendritic cells, macrophages → inflammatory mediators and cytokines.

sections.heading: Autophagy/lysosomes & ferroptosis
points: Lysosomes hold enzymes degrading proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids; acidic lumen (low pH) activates them.
Cathepsins L, B and D = abundant lysosomal proteases.
Ferroptosis: iron-dependent oxidation of PUFA-containing phospholipids → lipid peroxides → membrane disruption.
Protective systems: GPX4/glutathione (GSH), FSP1/coenzyme Q, DHFR/BH4; GPX4 reduces phospholipid hydroperoxides.
Some therapy-resistant cancer cells remain sensitive to ferroptosis induction.

mustRemember: Initiators: caspase-8 (extrinsic), caspase-9 (intrinsic); executioners: caspase-3, -6, -7
Intrinsic: stimulus → BAX/BAK → MOMP → cytochrome c → apoptosome → caspase-9 → caspase-3/7
Extrinsic: FasL → Fas → FADD → DISC → caspase-8 → caspase-3/7
BCL-2 = anti-apoptotic; BAX/BAK = pro-apoptotic effectors
BH1–BH4: effectors + anti-apoptotic; BH3-only: activators + sensitizers/derepressors
Apoptosis biochemical clues: caspase activation, DNA fragmentation, PS exposure
Necroptosis triggers: TNFR1, TLR3, TLR4 (extrinsic); ZBP1 + Z-nucleic acids (intrinsic)
Necroptosis → DAMP release → inflammation
Cathepsins L, B, D; lysosome activity needs acidic pH
Ferroptosis: Fe-dependent PUFA-phospholipid peroxidation; defenses GPX4/GSH, FSP1/CoQ, DHFR/BH4

distinguish.difference: Apoptosis: caspase-dependent, shrinkage, blebbing with intact membrane, non-inflammatory; necroptosis: caspase-independent, swelling, membrane rupture, DAMPs, inflammatory.
Intrinsic: internal stress → BAX/BAK, cytochrome c, apoptosome, caspase-9; extrinsic: Fas ligand → Fas → FADD/DISC → caspase-8.
Initiators (8, 9) start the cascade upstream; executioners (3, 6, 7) cleave cellular targets to dismantle the cell.
BCL-2 is anti-apoptotic and blocks permeabilization; BAX/BAK are pro-apoptotic effectors that permeabilize the mitochondrial outer membrane.
Effectors and anti-apoptotic members carry BH1–BH4; activators and sensitizers carry only BH3.
Ferroptosis is driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation (opposed by GPX4), not by the caspase cascade.

traps: Not every programmed death is apoptosis — necroptosis and ferroptosis are regulated but use different machinery and morphology.
Don't swap caspase-8 (extrinsic initiator) and caspase-9 (intrinsic initiator).
Blebbing with intact membrane = apoptosis; rupture + swelling + DAMP release = necroptosis.
BCL-2 is anti-apoptotic; BAX and BAK are pro-apoptotic.
Necroptosis is favored when caspase-8 is inhibited — blocking caspases doesn't necessarily save the cell.

oneLiner: Cancer cells proliferate without normal controls, evade apoptosis, invade and metastasize, and survive via a supportive microenvironment, hypoxia-driven HIF signaling, Warburg glycolysis and immune evasion (e.g., PD-1/PD-L1), which checkpoint blockade can reverse.

sections.heading: Origin, epidemiology and defining behaviors
points: Hippocrates' term karkinos (Greek: crab/crayfish) — tumor with outward-spreading veins like crab legs.
Carcinoma = cancer of epithelial tissue; malignant = capable of destructive growth and spread.
Incidence (new cases) ≠ mortality (deaths): high incidence does not imply equally high mortality.
Three defining behaviors: proliferation without normal growth-factor control, invasion through ECM/basement membrane, metastasis to distant sites.

sections.heading: Loss of growth and death controls
points: Homeostasis balances cell division with apoptosis; a tumor forms from ↑division, ↓apoptosis, or both.
Transformed cells lose contact inhibition → piled-up foci instead of an orderly monolayer.
Cancer cells bypass anchorage-dependent survival, surviving after leaving their normal tissue position.

sections.heading: Tumor microenvironment and hypoxia/HIF
points: Tumor = malignant cells + nonmalignant stroma (fibroblasts, immune cells, endothelial cells, other support cells).
Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) remodel ECM and secrete factors promoting growth, invasion, inflammation, angiogenesis.
O₂ falls with distance from vessels → hypoxia; severe hypoxia → necrosis.
Normoxia: HIF-α hydroxylated → recognized by VHL → ubiquitinated → proteasomal degradation.
Hypoxia: HIF-α stabilized → enters nucleus with HIF-β → activates angiogenesis, metabolism, erythropoiesis genes.

sections.heading: Pyruvate fates and the Warburg effect
points: Glycolysis: glucose → pyruvate (needs NAD⁺).
Aerobic: pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → citric acid cycle.
Anaerobic/hypoxic: pyruvate → lactate via lactate dehydrogenase (NADH → NAD⁺); yeast: ethanol + CO₂.
Warburg effect: cancer cells show high glucose uptake and pyruvate → lactate even when O₂ is available.
Lactate formation regenerates NAD⁺, sustaining continued glycolysis (metabolic reprogramming).

sections.heading: Immune evasion and PD-1/PD-L1 blockade
points: CD8 T cells recognize tumor antigens presented on MHC (via TCR).
Evasion: loss of tumor antigen or MHC, nonclassical HLA, inhibitory signals to T cells, immunosuppressive cytokines, suppressive cells (Treg, MDSC).
PD-L1 (tumor/immune cell) binds PD-1 (on T cell) → lowers T-cell activity.
Anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies (checkpoint inhibitors) block this → restore T-cell activity → tumor-cell death.

mustRemember: Karkinos = crab (Hippocrates)
Incidence = new cases; mortality = deaths
Hallmarks: uncontrolled proliferation, invasion, metastasis, reduced apoptosis, loss of contact inhibition, anchorage independence
Normoxia: HIF-α –OH → VHL → ubiquitin → degraded; hypoxia: HIF-α + HIF-β → angiogenesis/erythropoiesis/metabolism genes
Warburg: aerobic glycolysis → lactate; LDH regenerates NAD⁺
Stroma: fibroblasts (CAFs), immune cells, endothelial cells
Suppressive cells: Treg, MDSC
PD-1 on T cell; PD-L1 on tumor/immune cell; blockade ↑ T-cell activity

distinguish.difference: Invasion = local penetration through ECM/basement membrane; metastasis = spread from primary tumor to a new site.
Incidence counts new cases per period; mortality counts deaths per period.
Normoxia: hydroxylated HIF-α is VHL-targeted and degraded; hypoxia: HIF-α is stable and activates adaptive genes.
Normal aerobic cells send pyruvate to acetyl-CoA/TCA; Warburg cancer cells convert pyruvate to lactate despite O₂.
PD-1 is the inhibitory receptor on T cells; PD-L1 is its ligand on tumor/immune cells.

traps: Invasion and metastasis are not synonyms.
Tumors don't only arise from faster division — reduced apoptosis also causes net accumulation.
PD-1:PD-L1 binding suppresses T cells; checkpoint antibodies block the interaction to restore T-cell activity, not to block T cells.
Warburg effect occurs even when oxygen is present — it is not simply anaerobic fermentation due to hypoxia.
Tumor stroma is nonmalignant, yet it actively supports tumor progression.

oneLiner: Cancer arises from accumulated mutations activating oncogenes (EGFR, RAS) and inactivating tumor suppressors like p53 (restrained by MDM2/MDMX); the lecture then introduces oral formulation, absorption routes, bioavailability and ADME.

sections.heading: Mutagenesis and multistep cancer
points: Chemical carcinogens alter nucleotide sequences; X-rays cause chromosome breaks and translocations; UV damages specific DNA bases.
Cancer usually needs multiple rare, independent genetic and epigenetic changes.
The altered lineage descends from a single cell.
Epigenetic change = heritable change in gene activity without DNA-sequence change.

sections.heading: Oncogenes vs tumor suppressors; EGFR and RAS
points: Proto-oncogene → oncogene by gain-of-function; one altered allele can suffice (dominant).
Activation routes: coding/regulatory mutation, gene amplification, chromosome rearrangement.
Tumor suppressors act via loss of function; usually both copies must be inactivated (recessive at cell level).
EGF binds EGFR extracellular domain → intracellular domain phosphorylation; truncation → ligand-independent hyperphosphorylation/hyperactivation.
RAS GTPases (HRAS, NRAS, KRAS) signal when GTP-bound; mutant RAS stays in active GTP-bound state.

sections.heading: p53 and its regulators MDM2/MDMX
points: DNA damage ↑ p53 (transcription factor) → ↑ p21 → p21 inhibits cyclin-CDK → cell-cycle arrest for repair.
Cancer-associated p53 mutations disable its transcriptional tumor-suppressor function.
MDM2 and MDMX bind p53 and inhibit its transcriptional activity.
MDM2 (E3 ligase) promotes p53 nuclear export, ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
MDMX–MDM2 heterodimer enhances MDM2 E3 activity toward p53; the two also regulate each other's stability/ubiquitination.

sections.heading: Oral formulations and absorption
points: API may be only ~5–10% of an oral tablet/capsule; rest are excipients (fillers, lubricants, glidants, disintegration/dissolution aids).
Hard capsules: dry powders/pellets; soft capsules: oils or drug dissolved/suspended in oil.
Oral path: disintegration → dissolution → cross GI wall → portal vein → liver → systemic circulation.
Gut-wall and hepatic metabolism remove part of dose before systemic circulation, lowering bioavailability.

sections.heading: Routes of administration and ADME
points: IV enters blood directly, avoiding digestive-tract breakdown.
IM absorbed rapidly (muscle well vascularized); SC used for insulin and monoclonal antibodies; transdermal patches give controlled delivery; sublingual absorbed via mucosa under tongue.
Other routes: oral, inhaled, topical, epidural, rectal.
ADME = Absorption (site → blood), Distribution (blood → tissues), Metabolism (inactivate drug or activate prodrug; CYP450), Excretion (mainly kidney; also bile).
Bioavailability = fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation.

mustRemember: DNA damage → p53 → p21 ⊣ cyclin-CDK → arrest
MDM2: inhibits p53, nuclear export, ubiquitination, proteasomal degradation; MDMX: inhibits transactivation, heterodimer boosts MDM2 E3 activity
Oncogene = gain of function, one allele; tumor suppressor = loss of function, both alleles
Proto-oncogene activation: mutation, amplification, rearrangement
RAS family: HRAS, NRAS, KRAS (GTPases, active when GTP-bound)
Carcinogens: chemicals (sequence), X-rays (breaks/translocations), UV (base damage)
API ≈ 5–10% of oral formulation
Oral: disintegration → dissolution → GI wall → portal vein → liver (first-pass) → circulation
ADME; CYP450 = major drug-metabolizing enzyme family; main excretion = kidney

distinguish.difference: Oncogene: activating gain-of-function, one copy enough; tumor suppressor: loss-of-function, usually both copies lost.
Both inhibit p53 transactivation; MDM2 also ubiquitinates/exports/degrades p53, while MDMX enhances MDM2's E3 activity via heterodimer.
Hard hold dry powders/pellets; soft hold oils or drug in oil.
Disintegration = dosage form breaks into pieces; dissolution = drug molecules enter solution.
IV enters blood directly (no GI/first-pass loss); oral must be absorbed and survive gut-wall and hepatic metabolism.

traps: Don't reverse gene logic: oncogenes are activated drivers; tumor suppressors contribute when lost.
p53 is a tumor suppressor; MDM2/MDMX are its negative regulators (pro-cancer when overactive).
Bioavailability is the fraction reaching systemic circulation, not the amount swallowed or absorbed into portal blood.
Metabolism doesn't always inactivate — it can activate a prodrug.
A single mutation rarely causes cancer; multiple accumulated changes are usually needed.

oneLiner: Pharmacokinetics (ADME, the concentration–time curve with Cmax, tmax, t½, AUC) and drug metabolism (Phase I/II/III, paracetamol–glutathione safety story) set the stage for a high-attrition development pipeline that narrows ~10,000 candidates to one approved drug.

sections.heading: ADME revisited
points: Four linked stages: route/formulation affect absorption; blood flow and binding affect distribution; enzymes alter drug in metabolism; kidneys, bile, lungs, secretions excrete.
Distribution depends on blood flow, molecular size, lipophilicity, plasma-protein binding.
Kidney = main excretion route shown.
Prodrug = inactive/less active compound converted to active drug in the body.

sections.heading: Plasma concentration–time curve
points: Cmax = highest plasma concentration; tmax = time at which Cmax occurs.
t½ (half-life) = time for concentration to fall by half — how fast levels decline.
AUC = area under the curve = total drug exposure over time.

sections.heading: Drug metabolism reactions
points: Metabolism converts lipophilic drugs into more hydrophilic products for elimination.
Phase I (functionalization): hydroxylation, oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, dealkylation — introduce/expose functional groups.
Phase II (conjugation): glucuronidation, sulphonation, glutathione conjugation, methylation, acetylation — attach hydrophilic groups.
Outcome may be detoxification, activation, or a toxic metabolite.

sections.heading: Paracetamol and Phase III glutathione-conjugate handling
points: Most paracetamol → conjugated products; a minor route gives a reactive metabolite neutralized by glutathione.
Glutathione depletion increases danger from the reactive pathway.
Phase III: mercapturic acid pathway trims GSH conjugate → cysteine conjugate → N-acetylation → urinary excretion.
Competing β-lyase route on cysteine conjugates → reactive thiols → nephrotoxicity.

sections.heading: Drug-development pipeline and attrition
points: Discovery (target identification, validation, lead finding, lead optimization) → preclinical (short-term testing, formulation, PK) → clinical Phase I, II, III → regulatory approval (efficacy + safety review).
~10,000 candidates → ~250 preclinical → ~5 clinical → 1 drug.
Filters: target activity, safety, stability, solubility, reversibility, oral usefulness, patentability, manufacturability — potency alone is not enough.
Scale-up: surviving molecule must be manufactured safely at large scale.

mustRemember: Cmax = peak concentration; tmax = time to peak; t½ = time to halve; AUC = total exposure
Phase I: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, hydroxylation, dealkylation
Phase II: glucuronidation, sulphonation, GSH conjugation, methylation, acetylation
Phase III: mercapturic acid pathway → cysteine conjugate → N-acetyl → urine
β-lyase on cysteine conjugates → reactive thiols → nephrotoxicity
Paracetamol reactive metabolite detoxified by glutathione
Stages: discovery → preclinical → clinical (I, II, III) → regulatory approval
Distribution factors: blood flow, size, lipophilicity, plasma-protein binding

distinguish.difference: Cmax is the single highest concentration; AUC is total exposure integrated over time.
tmax is when the peak occurs; t½ is how long concentration takes to fall by half.

distinguish.pair: Phase I vs Phase II metabolism
distinguish.difference: Phase I introduces/exposes functional groups (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis); Phase II conjugates polar groups (glucuronide, sulphate, GSH).

distinguish.pair: Mercapturic acid route vs β-lyase route
distinguish.difference: Mercapturic acid: N-acetylated cysteine conjugate excreted in urine (safe); β-lyase: reactive thiols damaging kidney.
Preclinical tests safety/activity, formulation, PK before humans; clinical tests in humans through Phases I–III.

traps: Don't confuse Cmax (highest concentration) with AUC (total exposure).
Not every metabolic reaction is detoxification — some produce reactive/toxic metabolites (paracetamol, β-lyase thiols).
A hit/candidate is not an approved drug; potency alone does not make a drug.
Clinical Phases I–III are human trials — distinct from metabolic Phases I–III.

oneLiner: Drug discovery picks biomolecular targets and finds hits by computational (structure-/ligand-based) or high-throughput screening, illustrated by RAAS and the captopril story: venom peptide teprotide → first orally bioavailable ACE inhibitor with Zn²⁺-binding SAR.

sections.heading: Biomolecules as drug targets
points: Proteins: receptors, enzymes, carrier proteins, structural proteins (receptors and enzymes are key).
Nucleic acids: DNA and RNA.
Lipids form membranes; carbohydrates on cell surfaces aid recognition.

sections.heading: Computational (in-silico) screening
points: Virtual screening ranks molecules computationally before lab testing.
Structure-based: uses target 3D structure → docking, scoring, ranking.
Ligand-based: uses known ligands → similarity, pharmacophore, QSAR models.
Predicted hits must still be validated in a biological assay.

sections.heading: High-throughput screening (HTS)
points: Automated assays rapidly test very large compound libraries.
Primary hits → secondary assays (confirm) → dose-response → leads.
Leads are optimized by medicinal chemistry.
Hit = compound giving desired assay result; lead = promising hit selected for optimization.

sections.heading: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
points: Low blood pressure or low Na⁺ → renin released from kidney.
Renin → angiotensin I; ACE cleaves angiotensin I (peptide precursor) → angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone release → Na⁺/water retention → ↑ blood pressure.
ACE inhibitor ↓ angiotensin II formation → lowers blood pressure.

sections.heading: Captopril: discovery, binding and SAR
points: Bothrops jararaca (Brazilian pit viper) venom showed hypotensive activity.
Teprotide = nonapeptide (9 aa) ACE inhibitor from venom → peptide lead; analog studies → captopril, first orally bioavailable ACE inhibitor.
Binding: zinc-binding group coordinates catalytic Zn²⁺ (essential); carboxylate makes ionic + H-bond interactions; hydrophobic groups fill hydrophobic pockets.
SAR: N-ring must carry a carboxylic acid; larger hydrophobic N-rings improve potency and PK.
Zn-binding groups: thiol > carboxylate, phosphate; esterifying carboxylate/phosphate gives prodrugs.

mustRemember: Structure-based: docking/scoring; ligand-based: similarity, pharmacophore, QSAR
HTS: primary screen → secondary assay → dose-response → lead
RAAS: renin → Ang I → (ACE) → Ang II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone
Bothrops jararaca venom → teprotide (9-aa peptide) → captopril
Captopril = first orally bioavailable ACE inhibitor
Captopril contacts: Zn²⁺ coordination, carboxylate ionic/H-bond, hydrophobic pockets
Zn-binding strength: thiol > carboxylate/phosphate
Esterification → prodrug

distinguish.difference: Structure-based uses the target's 3D structure (docking); ligand-based uses known actives (similarity, pharmacophore, QSAR).
Virtual screening ranks compounds in silico; HTS experimentally tests large libraries with automated assays.
Hit = compound active in a screen; lead = confirmed, promising hit chosen for optimization.
Teprotide is the venom nonapeptide lead; captopril is the orally bioavailable small-molecule ACE inhibitor derived from it.
Ang I is the precursor made via renin; Ang II is the active ACE product causing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.

traps: Captopril is not the venom peptide — teprotide was the peptide lead.
Computational hits are predictions; they must be confirmed by biological assay.
A hit is not an approved drug.
ACE converts Ang I → Ang II; renin (not ACE) initiates the cascade.
Thiol, not carboxylate, is the strongest Zn²⁺-binding group in the SAR shown.

oneLiner: Drug discovery strategies (virtual, HTS and phenotypic screening, e.g., RAS-mutant selectivity by EC50), prodrug design and activation, and the thermal shift assay (TSA) as a protein-stability and ligand-binding readout.

sections.heading: Virtual and HTS workflows
points: Virtual screening starts from a protein structure or known active ligands → ranked hit list → biological assay for confirmation.
Computation ranks candidates; it does not prove activity.
HTS uses automated liquid handlers and detection: primary screen → secondary assays (remove false/nonreproducible hits) → dose-response → lead.

sections.heading: Phenotypic screening and RAS example
points: Selects compounds by an observable change in cells/organisms (e.g., halting proliferation); target need not be known first.
Target deconvolution may be needed afterwards; contrast target-based screening against a predefined target.
HRAS, KRAS, NRAS = small GTPases (GTP/GDP switch) in proliferation, growth, apoptosis; mutated in ~30% of human cancers.
EC50 = concentration giving half-maximal effect; lower EC50 = greater potency.
Compounds more potent (lower EC50) in HRAS-G12V mutant than wild-type cells → mutant-selective.

sections.heading: Ferroptosis as a phenotype
points: Regulated cell death from iron-associated oxidation of PUFA-containing phospholipids → lipid peroxides.
Iron uptake and lipoxygenase-linked reactions promote damage.
Glutathione-dependent peroxidase (GPX) and ferroptosis suppressor protein (FSP) pathways oppose it.

sections.heading: Prodrugs
points: Inactive/less active derivative converted to active drug in the body.
Fix poor solubility, absorption/permeability, instability, toxicity, bad taste, short duration; may enable new route or dosage form.
Promoiety = temporary group masking part of the drug, later removed.
Activation: enzymes (phosphatases, esterases, peptidases), chemical (hydrolysis, decarboxylation, light), or both.
Taste masking: bitter, water-soluble chloramphenicol → less soluble chloramphenicol palmitate, which dissolves less in the mouth.

sections.heading: Thermal shift assay (TSA)
points: Protein heated gradually; SYPRO Orange fluoresces upon binding hydrophobic surfaces exposed by unfolding.
Fluorescence rises during unfolding; Tm = midpoint of the transition; signal later falls as aggregates release dye.
Derivative plot locates the transition peak; RecA example shows pH alters Tm — higher Tm = more thermally stable.
Ligand binding preferentially to native fold stabilizes it → melt curve shifts to higher Tm (positive thermal shift).

mustRemember: EC50 = half-maximal effect concentration; lower EC50 = more potent
RAS (HRAS/KRAS/NRAS) mutated in ~30% human cancers; HRAS-G12V example
Phenotypic screening: target unknown → later target deconvolution
Prodrug activators: phosphatase, esterase, peptidase; hydrolysis, decarboxylation, light
Chloramphenicol → chloramphenicol palmitate (taste masking)
TSA dye: SYPRO Orange binds exposed hydrophobic surfaces
Tm = midpoint of unfolding; higher Tm = more stable
Ligand binding → positive ΔTm

distinguish.difference: Phenotypic selects by observable cell/organism effect without knowing target; target-based screens against a predefined molecular target.
Primary finds possible hits at large scale; secondary confirms and characterizes them, removing false positives.
Enzymatic uses esterases/phosphatases/peptidases; chemical uses hydrolysis, decarboxylation or light.

distinguish.pair: Fluorescence rise vs fall in TSA
distinguish.difference: Rise = unfolding exposes hydrophobic sites binding SYPRO Orange; fall = aggregation releases dye.

traps: Lower EC50 means greater potency, not weaker activity.
A TSA Tm shift supports ligand binding but is not a full affinity measurement and doesn't locate the binding site.
Virtual screening outputs a ranked hit list — not proof of activity.
The taste-masking prodrug works by reducing water solubility, not by adding a sweet group.

oneLiner: Biophysical methods for stability and interactions: TSA (Tm shift), isothermal titration calorimetry (heat of binding → Ka, n, ΔH; c-value), and FRET (distance-dependent energy transfer, e.g., cameleon Ca²⁺ sensor), with p53–MDM2 and Bcl-2 as interaction targets.

sections.heading: TSA signal and binding readout
points: Heating unfolds protein → exposed hydrophobic regions bind SYPRO Orange → fluorescence ↑.
Tm read at transition midpoint; aggregation at higher temperature releases dye → signal ↓.
Compare protein ± ligand: positive Tm shift = stabilizing interaction.
Detects stability change, not the binding site.

sections.heading: ITC setup and titration
points: Sample cell (protein) and reference cell (buffer) in insulated jacket; instrument detects tiny temperature differences.
Measures feedback power needed to keep both cells at same temperature as binding releases/absorbs heat.
Exothermic binding (ΔH < 0) → sample-cell feedback power decreases; endothermic → increases.
Early injections: binding sites mostly free → large peaks; signal returns to baseline before next injection.
As sites fill, peaks shrink; at saturation signal is mainly heat of dilution.

sections.heading: Reading ITC data and c-value
points: Raw trace: one peak per injection (power vs time); integrate each peak → heat per injection.
Plot heat vs ligand:protein molar ratio → binding isotherm.
Plateau → ΔH; inflection point → stoichiometry (n); slope → affinity (Ka); Ka = 1/Kd.
c = n[P]Ka controls sigmoidicity; a sigmoidal isotherm is needed for accurate fitting.
Ligand-into-buffer dilution control measured separately and subtracted.

sections.heading: Interaction targets: p53–MDM2/MDMX and Bcl-2
points: MDM2 and MDMX negatively regulate tumor suppressor p53.
MDM2 binds p53 → ubiquitination, nuclear export, proteasomal degradation → ↓ p53 target-gene expression.
Bcl-2 family (pro- and anti-apoptotic members) interact at mitochondrial membrane; balance decides permeabilization → caspase activation.

sections.heading: FRET and the cameleon Ca²⁺ sensor
points: Nonradiative energy transfer from excited donor to nearby acceptor fluorophore.
Requires donor emission/acceptor absorption spectral overlap and short distance (usually within ~10 nm).
E = 1/[1 + (r/R₀)⁶]; R₀ (Förster radius) = distance at 50% efficiency; efficiency falls steeply with distance.
Cameleon: CFP–calmodulin–M13–YFP; genetically encoded Ca²⁺ sensor in living cells.
No Ca²⁺ → weak FRET, cyan emission; Ca²⁺ → calmodulin binds M13 → CFP/YFP close → FRET ↑ → yellow emission.

mustRemember: TSA: SYPRO Orange, Tm = transition midpoint, ligand → +ΔTm
ITC gives Ka (affinity), n (stoichiometry), ΔH (enthalpy) from one experiment
Ka = 1/Kd
c = n[P]Ka (needs sigmoidal isotherm)
Exothermic: ΔH < 0, feedback power ↓; endothermic: power ↑
Isotherm: plateau → ΔH, inflection → n, slope → Ka
After saturation: heat of dilution only; subtract ligand-into-buffer control
FRET E = 1/[1 + (r/R₀)⁶]; R₀ = 50% efficiency; ~10 nm range
Cameleon: CFP donor, YFP acceptor, calmodulin + M13; Ca²⁺ → yellow

distinguish.difference: TSA measures fluorescence-based thermal stability (Tm shift); ITC measures binding heat to give Ka, n and ΔH.
Exothermic releases heat (ΔH < 0, feedback power decreases); endothermic absorbs heat (feedback power increases).
Ka = association constant (larger = tighter); Kd = dissociation constant; Ka = 1/Kd.
Early: many free sites, large peaks; late: saturated sites, small peaks from heat of dilution.
Donor (e.g., CFP) supplies excitation energy; acceptor (e.g., YFP) receives it and emits.
Without Ca²⁺: weak FRET, cyan emission; with Ca²⁺: calmodulin–M13 binding, strong FRET, yellow emission.

traps: ITC heat peaks are power-vs-time signals, not concentrations — integrate before fitting the isotherm.
TSA Tm shift indicates stabilization but is not a complete affinity or binding-site measurement.
FRET needs both proximity (~10 nm) and spectral overlap; co-expression of donor and acceptor doesn't prove interaction.
FRET efficiency varies with the sixth power of distance — not linearly.
Late-titration signal is heat of dilution, not binding; it must be subtracted via a ligand-into-buffer control.
